newsitem.title: USA: Dow Chemical shares rebound after jury verdict.
newsitem.headline: Dow Chemical shares rebound after jury verdict.

text.p: Shares of Dow Chemical Co. rebounded slightly on Tuesday as investors discounted the threat that Monday's breast implant verdict against the company would eventually lead to billions of dollars in damages.

But analysts conceded that the Midland, Mich.-based chemical giant is likely to remain mired in silicone breast implant litigation for a long time to come -- much like the protracted legal battles over tobacco and asbestos.
Dow shares sank $3 on the news Monday, but Tuesday gained 75 cents to close at $90.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"This appears to be the kind of litigation that will eventually spiral its way to the U.S. Supreme Court," said Larry Dubin, a law professor at the University of Detroit-Mercy. "Yesterday's decision indicates that plaintiffs have a favorable case to sell to juries, if they can get to juries."

In the first phase of a class-action suit, a state court jury in New Orleans found that the chemical giant was negligent in testing silicone for use in human implants and that it intentionally withheld information about the dangers of such silicone implants.

The decision clears the way for the trial's second phase, in which the same jury will consider what many analysts believe to be a more important question -- whether the implants actually made eight women who received them ill with autoimmune and connective tissue disorders such as aches, fevers and Lupus. That phase starts Sept. 29.

The eight plaintiffs represent a class of 1,800 women who received implants from Dow Corning Corp., the 50-50 joint venture between Dow Chemical and Corning Inc. that was once the nation's largest maker of breast implants.

Dow Corning filed for bankruptcy protection in 1995, forcing plaintiffs to turn to Dow Chemical for recourse on the theory that it performed silicone testing for Dow Corning worker safety in the 1940s and 1950s.

Dow Chemical has based a major part of its defense on the fact that it neither made nor tested breast implants, which failed to deter the jury on Monday. The second pillar of its defense -- that there is no conclusive scientific evidence that implants cause disease -- has not been fully tested.
The New Orleans case is the first class action breast implant case to come to trial, but Dow Chemical has lost two other trials involving individual plaintiffs.
A Houston judge threw out a jury verdict against Dow in 1995, and a $14 million verdict against the company in Reno, Nev., has been appealed to the Nevada Supreme Court.

Analysts said they believe Dow Chemical will find a way to settle the litigation long before it threatens to crush the $20 billion-a-year chemical giant. The company has had more than 4,000 suits against it dismissed and succeeded in getting the bulk of the 1,800 Louisiana plantiffs' cases moved to Michigan.
"The issue is not one where Dow Chemical could be brought down, because you'll never get to the point where that could happen," said Smith Barney Inc. analyst James Wilbur.
He added that resolution of the Dow Corning bankruptcy case could provide a framework for much of the litigation involving the two companies to be settled.
Dow Corning has until Aug. 26 to file its amended reorganization plan, which is expected to provide a new formula for payment of claims for women with legitimate health problems.
Dow Chemical spokesman John Musser said the company is giving "absolutely no consideration to any settlements," and intends to keep fighting in court.
Plaintiff groups, emboldened by their victory, also are talking tough.

"I think Dow Chemical is in for the rudest awakening they've ever had," said Sybil Niden Goldrich, a former implant recipient and a self-appointed spokeswoman for plaintiff groups. She added that if Dow Chemical had provided money for women to have their implants removed, "they would have mollified a lot of these people."
